content: Salvia sclarea, commonly known as clary or clary sage, is a biennial or short-lived perennial herb belonging to the genus Salvia. It is native to regions spanning Europe to central Asia. This plant typically grows to a height of approximately 1 meter. Its leaves are arranged oppositely, measuring between 10 to 20 centimeters in length and 6 to 12 centimeters in width, and they possess a thick, woolly texture. The flowers of Salvia sclarea are organized in clusters of 2 to 6 along the stem.5 to 3.5 centimeters in length and exhibits colors ranging from white to pink or pale purple. The plant emits a strong and distinctive odor, which some individuals find unpleasant, while others consider it highly appealing. The essential oil derived from Salvia sclarea is occasionally available in specialty stores, such as natural food shops or stores dedicated to fragrances. The scent of this oil is often described as sweaty, spicy, or reminiscent of hay. The seeds of clary sage are coated with a mucilaginous substance, which led to their historical use in herbal medicine. Specifically, old herbal texts recommended placing a seed into the eye of an individual with a foreign object lodged in it, as the mucilaginous coating would adhere to the object, facilitating its removal. The leaves of Salvia sclarea have been utilized as a vegetable in culinary practices. Historically, clary sage was employed as a flavoring agent in ales before the widespread adoption of hops. It was also used to flavor certain wines, particularly muscatel. Additionally, clary sage has been incorporated as a flavoring in some tobacco products. The plant can be prepared as a tea or used in aromatherapy, where it is believed to exert a calming effect. Furthermore, clary sage serves as the primary ingredient in Norambrolide, a dietary supplement marketed with unsubstantiated claims regarding its ability to promote fat catabolism.
